_comment: A look, as a set of numbers. Every look in the game is one of these — there is
no longer such a thing as a look that is only a shader, which is what used to
make `toon` and its four siblings impossible to save and impossible to leave.
`shader` names one of the five quantisers in comic_look.gdshaderinc: how the
surface steps from its shadow into the sun. Everything else in the pipeline is
shared, so everything else is a number here.
A value is read by its JSON type. A number is a float; a "#rrggbb" string is
a colour, and it reaches the shader as the exact components it spells — Godot
does not convert a Color set from script on a `source_color` uniform, which was
measured rather than assumed. Nothing else is accepted, so a typo here is inert
rather than a creature that quietly looks wrong.
**A preset is read as complete.** `Look.wear` puts the whole shared vocabulary
back to the shader's own defaults before applying one, so anything left out here
is the default and not whatever the last look happened to leave behind. Leaving
that out is how switching looks used to accumulate: `comic-sunday` sets the
saturation to 1.55, `toon` set nothing at all, and the toon look inherited it.
These win over the sliders on the creature — saturation and the rest. A preset
is a deliberate statement about a look, and a slider is not a good reason to

bd._note: Franco-Belgian album: one hard terminator, flattened fills, one screen and an inked fold. The ink is a near-black blue-violet rather than black, which is what a two-colour press puts down and what keeps a fold line from reading as a hole in the page.

comic-clear._note: Ligne claire. No tone at all, two flat fills, and the whole read carried by the line. Tintin, Spirou: the discipline is that nothing is hatched, so the drawing has to be right.

comic-manga._note: Tone does the structural work, in fine screens over a deep core — but the paint keeps its colour. Swept 0.85 / 1.05 / 1.25 / 1.45 on two creatures: under 1.05 the difference from the desaturated original barely reads, over 1.35 the warm bodies go hot and the screen starts fighting the fill. Back to 1.0 once the missing 1/pi was found (decision 0067): every number above 1 here was fighting a pipeline that was 3.14 times too bright.

comic-newsprint._note: Cheap press: a coarse screen you are meant to see, four inks, warm paper grey in the shadow. The posterise is on here and nowhere else in the comic family.

comic-noir._note: Most of the form in shadow and the light as the exception. The terminator is pushed past the middle, so the lit side becomes a shape rather than a default.

comic-sunday._note: The bright end. Little shadow, saturated fills, a light screen at a shallow angle. Closest of the family to what a game for children would actually ship.

ramp._note: The whole light response read off `shading_ramp.png`. Nothing else shades it, so nothing else is turned on — this look is the strip, and editing the strip is how it is changed.

toon._note: Three flat bands, a fold line, a stepped highlight and a rim. The cel look: nothing is printed, so no screen and no terminator stroke. Was a shader of its own with nineteen uniforms prefixed `toon_`; every one of them turned out to be a general question already asked elsewhere under another name.

typelit._note: Two tones in the creature's own element colour, and a rim in it too. The shadow is the element darkened rather than grey, which is what makes the pair read as one creature instead of as a creature and a stain. The same quantiser as `bd`: what separates them is entirely numbers, which is the point of writing them down here.

vinyl._note: A gradient, warm into cool, and nothing stepped anywhere. The whole point is that the terminator is not a statement, so every mark in the ink stage is off.
